n: Lehi now blesses Jacob, his first son born in the wilderness. As a child Jacob suffered because of his older brothers’ harshness.

f.w: my firstborn in the days of my tribulation

n: Jacob knows God’s greatness, and Lehi promises that God will “consecrate” his afflictions — turn his suffering into something sacred and beneficial.

f.w: he shall consecrate thine afflictions for thy gain

n: Jacob will be blessed, live safely with Nephi, and serve God all his days. Lehi knows Jacob is redeemed — not by Jacob’s own goodness, but by the righteousness of his Redeemer, whom Jacob has seen will come.

f.w: because of the righteousness of thy Redeemer

f.g: The appointed time in God’s plan.

n: Jacob saw Christ’s glory as a youth, so he is as blessed as those who will see Christ in mortality. The Spirit is unchanging. Since the Fall, the way back has been prepared, and salvation is “free” — offered as a gift to all.

f.w: thou hast beheld in thy youth his glory

n: People know good from evil, and God has given law. But no one is made right with God by the law alone, because everyone breaks it. Under both temporal and spiritual law, people are cut off and become miserable.

f.w: instructed sufficiently that they know good from evil
by the law no flesh is justified

n: So redemption comes only through the Holy Messiah, who is full of grace and truth.
Christ offered Himself as a sacrifice for sin to satisfy the demands of the law — for all who have a broken heart and a contrite spirit. Repentance opens the door to His Atonement.

f.w: answer the ends of the law
a broken heart and a contrite spirit

n: How important it is to teach everyone that no one can live with God except through Christ’s merits, mercy, and grace. He lays down His life and takes it up again, bringing about the resurrection as the first to rise.
Christ is the “firstfruits” — the first of the harvest of the resurrection. He intercedes, or pleads, for all people, and those who believe in Him will be saved.

f.g: The first part of a harvest, offered to God; here, the first to be resurrected.

n: Because of Christ’s intercession, all people return to God to be judged by Him. Punishment and happiness are both “affixed” — attached as consequences — to the law, and both serve the purposes of the Atonement. The sentence continues into the next verse.

A foundational idea: there must be opposition in all things. Without opposites, there could be no righteousness or wickedness, joy or misery. Everything would be one undivided “compound,” lifeless and meaningless.

f.g: A single undifferentiated mass, with no contrasts.

n: Such a world would have been created for nothing, with no purpose — which would undermine God’s wisdom, purposes, power, mercy, and justice.

A chain of logic: no law means no sin; no sin, no righteousness; no righteousness, no happiness; and without these there is no God — and nothing would exist at all. Moral law and existence itself are tied together.

f.w: to act nor to be acted upon

n: But there is a God. He created the heavens and the earth and everything in them — both things that act (agents) and things that are acted upon.
To accomplish His purposes for humanity, God placed opposition in Eden: the forbidden fruit opposite the tree of life, one sweet and one bitter.

f.w: the forbidden fruit in opposition to the tree of life

n: God gave humanity agency — the power to act for themselves. But real choice requires being “enticed” by both good and evil.
From scripture, Lehi concludes that an angel of God fell from heaven and became the devil by seeking evil.

Having become miserable, the devil wants everyone to be miserable. As the serpent and “father of all lies,” he told Eve she would not die but would become like God, knowing good and evil — a half-truth wrapped around a lie.
After eating the forbidden fruit, Adam and Eve were sent out of Eden to work the ground.

f.w: driven out of the garden of Eden

n: They had children — the whole human family.

f.w: the family of all the earth

n: God lengthened human life so people could repent while in mortality. Life became a “state of probation” — a test. All must repent, because the Fall left everyone lost.
Had Adam not transgressed, he and Eve would have stayed in Eden, and everything would have remained unchanged forever. Latter-day Saints often distinguish this “transgression” from sin.
They would have had no children and stayed innocent — with no joy because they knew no misery, and doing no good because they knew no sin.

f.w: they would have had no children

n: All this happened according to the wisdom of God, who knows all things. The Fall was part of His plan, not a failure of it.

f.w: the wisdom of him who knoweth all things

n: One of the best-known verses in the Book of Mormon: Adam fell so that humanity could exist, and people exist so that they can have joy. Joy is the purpose of our existence.

f.w: Adam fell that men might be

n: The Messiah will come to redeem humanity from the Fall. Redeemed, people are forever free to act for themselves rather than being acted upon — accountable only to God’s law at the last day.

f.w: to act for themselves and not to be acted upon

n: Because of Christ, people are free to choose liberty and eternal life through Him, the great Mediator, or captivity and death through the devil, who wants everyone to be as miserable as he is.

f.w: free to choose liberty and eternal life

f.g: One who stands between two parties to reconcile them.

n: Lehi pleads with his sons to look to the Mediator, obey His commandments, and choose eternal life by following the Holy Spirit.
Don’t choose eternal death by following the flesh and its evil, which gives the devil power to drag you down and rule over you.
Near the end of his life, Lehi says he has “chosen the good part” — echoing scripture — and his only aim is his sons’ eternal welfare.
